original_question: Suppose f : (-infinity, 0] x R^3 -> [0, infinity) is a smooth classical solution of the space-homogeneous Landau-Coulomb equation, satisfies 0 <= f(t, v) <= 1 everywhere, and for every time t there is a constant C_t with integral f(v) <v>^{-1} dv <= C_t. Must f be a stationary Maxwellian?
target_in_paper: Section 7.2, Conjecture 7.5: the Liouville-type conjecture that any bounded ancient smooth solution of the space-homogeneous Landau-Coulomb equation in R^3, with the mild weighted L^1 condition needed to define the coefficients, must be a stationary Maxwellian.
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's actual target. It correctly identifies the homogeneous Landau-Coulomb setting in three velocity dimensions, the ancient time interval (-infinity,0], the smooth classical solution class, the pointwise bound 0 <= f <= 1, the time-dependent weighted integrability assumption with weight <v>^{-1}, and the intended conclusion that f should be a stationary Maxwellian. In substance, it matches Conjecture 7.5 almost line by line.
missing_details: The question should explicitly state the PDE itself, namely that f is an ancient solution of the space-homogeneous Landau equation \partial_t f = Q(f,f) with the Landau-Coulomb collision operator.
To be stand-alone, the Landau-Coulomb operator Q should be defined (for example via the standard kernel a(z)=|z|^{-1}(I-z\otimes z/|z|^2) in the divergence form of the homogeneous Landau operator).
The weighted integrability hypothesis should be quantified as: for every t <= 0 there exists C_t < infinity such that \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} f(t,v)\langle v\rangle^{-1} dv <= C_t.
The notation \langle v\rangle should be defined explicitly as (1+|v|^2)^{1/2}.
It helps to say explicitly that this is an ancient-solution/Liouville question, since that is the role of the conjecture in the paper's blow-up analysis.
The conclusion should clarify what 'stationary Maxwellian' means: a time-independent Maxwellian equilibrium of the Landau-Coulomb equation.

A paper-faithful stand-alone version should mention that the weighted L^1 assumption is not decorative: the note immediately after Conjecture 7.5 says it is needed just to make sense of the coefficient formula in the operator.
refined_question:
Let f:(-\infty,0]\times \mathbb{R}^3 \to [0,\infty) be a smooth classical ancient solution of the space-homogeneous Landau equation with Coulomb potential, \partial_t f = Q(f,f), where Q is the standard Landau-Coulomb collision operator in velocity space, for instance
Q(f,f)(v)=\nabla_v\cdot \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |v-v_*|^{-1}\Big(I-\frac{(v-v_*)\otimes (v-v_*)}{|v-v_*|^2}\Big)\big(f(v_*)\nabla_v f(v)-f(v)\nabla_{v_*}f(v_*)\big)\,dv_*.
Assume that 0 <= f(t,v) <= 1 for every (t,v) in (-\infty,0]\times \mathbb{R}^3, and that for every t <= 0 there exists a constant C_t < \infty such that
\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} f(t,v)\langle v\rangle^{-1}\,dv \le C_t, \qquad \langle v\rangle=(1+|v|^2)^{1/2}.
Must f be a stationary Maxwellian, i.e. a time-independent Maxwellian equilibrium of the Landau-Coulomb equation?
justification: The draft is not aiming at the main regularity theorems from earlier sections; it clearly targets the speculative blow-up/Liouville discussion in Section 7.2. The paper first sets up the space-homogeneous equation in Section 7 via equation (7.1) and recalls the Landau-Coulomb operator in equation (7.2). It then develops a blow-up-limit heuristic: after Proposition 7.2 and the radial blow-up analysis using Lemma 7.4, the author writes that it is reasonable to expect that the only bounded ancient solutions are stationary Maxwellians, and immediately states this precisely as Conjecture 7.5. Your hypotheses and conclusion match that conjecture, not the preceding Conjecture 7.3. The note right after Conjecture 7.5 adds an important hidden point: the weighted L^1 assumption is needed just to make sense of the coefficient formula in the operator. That is why the refined version mainly needs operator and notation definitions, not a change of mathematical scope.
